triage.name: Appendicitis
triage.reason: Classic undifferentiated abdominal pain case with a clear diagnosis reachable by history, exam, labs and imaging, and important look-alikes.

demographics: Most common cause of acute abdominal pain requiring surgery in the US
family_history: Appendicitis in a parent or sibling

chief_complaints.text: The pain started near my belly button and moved down to the right side
I feel sick to my stomach

hpi.onset: Gradual, over several hours; not instantaneous
hpi.duration: Usually less than 48 hours by the time people come in
hpi.progression: Vague pain around the belly button first, then it settles in the right lower abdomen over 12–24 hours and becomes steady and worse; it hurts more with movement
hpi.location: Periumbilical at first, then right lower quadrant
hpi.quality: Dull and crampy early, then sharp and constant once it localizes
hpi.severity: Moderate and worsening; about 6–8/10 by presentation
hpi.timing: Constant once localized; no pain-free stretches
aggravating: Going over bumps in the car
relieving: Lying still with the knees bent

associated_symptoms.text: Vomiting that started after the pain

pertinent_negatives: Flank pain that comes in waves
Vaginal bleeding or a missed period
Sick contacts with the same illness

negatives: Yellowing of the eyes or skin
argues_against: Vomiting that came before the pain
Colicky flank pain radiating to the groin
Sudden one-sided pelvic pain with vomiting

atypical.how_it_differs: Young children cannot describe the pain moving; they show up irritable, vomiting, and refusing to walk or be touched.
Pain is milder, fever may be low or absent, and the white count can be near normal even when the appendix is already perforated.
As the uterus grows the appendix is pushed upward, so pain may be in the right flank or upper right abdomen and nausea and vomiting are blamed on pregnancy.
Thicker abdominal wall makes the exam less reliable and imaging harder to interpret, so pain may feel less localized and the exam less impressive than the disease.

general.mild: Uncomfortable but not ill-appearing; lies still and prefers not to move
general.moderate: Lies still with knees drawn up, winces when the stretcher is bumped or with coughing
general.severe: Ill-appearing and flushed, reluctant to move, guarded when approached
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, pale and diaphoretic, quiet or lethargic, peritonitic

findings.maneuver: Palpate all four quadrants, starting in the quadrant farthest from the pain and saving the right lower quadrant for last
findings.finding: Tenderness localized to the right lower quadrant

findings.maneuver: Press at McBurney point, about one-third of the way from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus
findings.finding: Focal point tenderness at McBurney point

findings.maneuver: Palpate the right lower quadrant gently
findings.finding: Voluntary guarding of the abdominal wall muscles

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to cough, or gently tap the heel or bump the stretcher
findings.finding: Sharp pain in the right lower quadrant with jarring, suggesting peritoneal irritation

findings.maneuver: Press slowly and deeply in the right lower quadrant, then release quickly
findings.finding: Pain worse on release than on pressing

findings.maneuver: Press in the left lower quadrant
findings.finding: Pain referred to the right lower quadrant

findings.maneuver: With the patient on the left side, extend the right hip
findings.finding: Right lower quadrant pain, suggesting a retrocecal appendix

findings.maneuver: Flex the right hip and knee and internally rotate the hip
findings.finding: Hypogastric or pelvic pain, suggesting a pelvic appendix
Diffuse rigidity with involuntary guarding, suggesting generalized peritonitis

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the abdomen in all four quadrants
Palpate for an abdominal mass and percuss the liver span
findings.finding: No discrete mass and normal liver span

findings.maneuver: Perform a pelvic exam when a gynecologic cause is possible
findings.finding: No cervical motion tenderness, no adnexal mass or tenderness

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the groins and umbilicus with the patient coughing

labs.caveat: A normal white count does not rule out appendicitis, especially early or in older adults.
Rises more after 24 hours; higher values suggest perforation.
Mild sterile pyuria from an inflamed appendix next to the ureter or bladder; can mislead toward a urinary infection.
Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging; rules out ectopic pregnancy.

findings.finding: No ischemic ST-segment or T-wave changes; ECG is not needed to diagnose appendicitis and is obtained only to evaluate chest pain or rule out a cardiac cause of upper abdominal pain

imaging.study: Ultrasound of the right lower quadrant
CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast

findings.text: Dilated appendix over 6 mm with wall thickening and enhancement

imaging.study: MRI abdomen and pelvis without contrast

findings.text: Usually nonspecific; occasionally a calcified appendicolith

initial.why: Leukocytosis with left shift supports inflammation
Looks for urinary infection or a stone
Rules out pregnancy and ectopic pregnancy before imaging

initial.test: Ultrasound of the right lower quadrant

confirmatory.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
confirmatory.why: Most accurate test in nonpregnant adults

supporting.why: Adds to the white count in scoring and suggests perforation when high

supporting.test: MRI abdomen and pelvis without contrast

not_indicated.why: No role in right lower quadrant pain
Not needed unless the pain is epigastric

decision_points: Pregnancy test before CT in anyone who could be pregnant
Ultrasound first in children and pregnancy; CT if nondiagnostic in nonpregnant patients
Peritonitis or instability goes to surgery without waiting for imaging

differential.name: Ectopic pregnancy
differential.why_considered: Lower abdominal pain in a patient who could be pregnant; can mimic appendicitis closely and is life-threatening.
differential.trigger: Any patient of childbearing potential with abdominal pain, especially with a missed period or vaginal bleeding.

history: Pain may be sudden and severe
Prior ectopic pregnancy or tubal surgery
imaging: No intrauterine pregnancy on transvaginal ultrasound

differential.name: Ovarian torsion
differential.why_considered: Sudden one-sided lower abdominal pain with nausea and vomiting, often in a young patient.
differential.trigger: Abrupt onset of severe one-sided pelvic pain with vomiting at the start.

history: Sudden onset, often while moving or exercising
labs: White count may be mildly elevated
imaging: Enlarged ovary with reduced or absent Doppler flow on ultrasound

differential.name: Pelvic inflammatory disease
differential.why_considered: Lower abdominal pain and fever in a sexually active patient.

imaging: Tubal thickening or fluid on ultrasound; often normal

differential.name: Viral gastroenteritis
differential.why_considered: Nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain are common in both conditions.

history: Vomiting or diarrhea before the pain
Diffuse crampy pain rather than focal
imaging: Not routinely needed; normal appendix if imaged

differential.name: Kidney stone
differential.why_considered: Right-sided abdominal or flank pain with nausea and vomiting.

history: Colicky flank pain radiating to the groin
exam: No focal right lower quadrant peritoneal signs
imaging: Stone and hydronephrosis on CT or ultrasound

differential.name: Mesenteric adenitis
differential.why_considered: Right lower quadrant pain in a child or young adult, often after a viral illness.

history: Diffuse or migratory pain without classic migration to the right lower quadrant
labs: White count normal or mildly elevated
imaging: Enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes with a normal appendix on ultrasound or CT

differential.name: Crohn disease
differential.why_considered: Right lower quadrant pain from terminal ileitis can mimic appendicitis.

history: Family history of inflammatory bowel disease
exam: Right lower quadrant tenderness without acute peritoneal signs
imaging: Terminal ileum wall thickening and inflammation on CT or MRI enterography

differential.name: Diverticulitis
differential.why_considered: Left or lower abdominal pain with fever and leukocytosis; can present on the right in some patients.

history: Left lower quadrant pain more typical
Constipation or change in bowel habit
imaging: Diverticula with pericolic fat stranding on CT

severity.mild: Early, uncomplicated appendicitis: less than 24 hours of symptoms, localized right lower quadrant tenderness, low-grade or no fever, mild leukocytosis.
severity.moderate: Established, uncomplicated appendicitis: clear migration of pain, guarding, fever, and marked leukocytosis.
severity.severe: Perforated appendicitis with a localized abscess or phlegmon: high fever, persistent pain, palpable mass, and marked leukocytosis.
severity.critical: Free perforation with generalized peritonitis and sepsis: rigid abdomen, hypotension, tachycardia, and altered mental status.

red_flags.meaning: Generalized peritonitis; needs urgent surgical evaluation.
Sepsis; resuscitate and involve surgery immediately.

red_flags.finding: Sudden relief of pain followed by worse, spreading pain

red_flags.meaning: Severe infection or sepsis, especially in older adults.

complications.name: Adhesive small bowel obstruction
clues: Prior appendectomy with new distension and vomiting

complications.name: Surgical site infection
clues: Wound redness, warmth, or drainage after appendectomy

special_populations.differences: Younger children cannot describe pain migration and often present irritable, vomiting, and refusing to walk; perforation rates are higher because diagnosis is delayed. Ultrasound is first-line imaging.
Findings are often atypical and milder; fever may be low or absent and the white count can be near normal even with perforation. Perforation rates are higher.

Appendicitis is the most common non-obstetric surgical emergency in pregnancy. The growing uterus pushes the appendix upward, so pain may be in the right flank or upper right abdomen, and nausea and vomiting may be attributed to pregnancy. Ultrasound first, then MRI if nondiagnostic.
A thicker abdominal wall makes the exam less reliable and imaging harder to interpret; pain may feel less localized and the exam less impressive than the underlying disease.
May have blunted fever and leukocytosis and can progress rapidly to perforation; maintain a lower threshold for imaging.

key_questions.question: Where did the pain start, and has it moved since then?
key_questions.looking_for: Pain that began around the belly button and then settled in the right lower abdomen

key_questions.question: When did the pain start, and is it getting better or worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over hours, steadily worsening, usually less than 48 hours

key_questions.question: Is the pain constant or does it come and go?
key_questions.looking_for: Constant once it localizes, with no pain-free stretches

key_questions.question: Does anything make it worse, like walking, coughing, or going over bumps in the car?
key_questions.looking_for: Pain worse with movement or jarring, suggesting peritoneal irritation

key_questions.question: Does anything make it feel better?
key_questions.looking_for: Lying still with the knees bent

key_questions.question: Did the vomiting start before or after the pain began?
key_questions.looking_for: Vomiting after the pain; vomiting first points toward gastroenteritis

key_questions.question: Have you had any diarrhea?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent or mild; profuse watery diarrhea argues against appendicitis

key_questions.question: Have you felt warm or had chills?
Have you been able to pass gas or have a bowel movement?
key_questions.looking_for: Inability to pass gas or constipation

key_questions.question: Any burning with urination, blood in the urine, or pain in your side or back?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests a urinary cause such as a stone or infection

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Excludes ectopic pregnancy in anyone of childbearing potential

key_questions.question: Any vaginal discharge, bleeding, or pain with intercourse?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests pelvic inflammatory disease or an ectopic pregnancy

key_questions.question: Have you had your appendix removed, or any other abdominal surgery?
Has anyone in your family had appendicitis?
key_questions.looking_for: Appendicitis in a parent or sibling

key_questions.question: Has anyone around you had the same stomach illness?
key_questions.looking_for: Sick contacts, which would point toward gastroenteritis

key_questions.question: Has the pain suddenly gotten much worse or spread across your whole belly?
key_questions.looking_for: Sudden worsening or diffuse pain suggesting perforation and peritonitis

reasoning_points: Pain that migrates from the periumbilical area to the right lower quadrant
Anorexia with vomiting that began after the pain
Localized right lower quadrant tenderness with peritoneal signs such as guarding, rebound, or pain with coughing
Low-grade fever and leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance
Pregnancy excluded with a negative hCG before imaging
Imaging showing a dilated, noncompressible appendix with surrounding inflammation
Look-alikes considered and addressed, including ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion, pelvic inflammatory disease, gastroenteritis, kidney stone, mesenteric adenitis, and Crohn disease

easy: Teenager or young adult with the classic migration story
CT or ultrasound confirms an inflamed appendix
medium: Retrocecal appendix with flank pain, a positive psoas sign, and little anterior tenderness
Mild sterile pyuria on urinalysis that could mislead toward a urinary infection
Woman of reproductive age with gynecologic look-alikes requiring a pregnancy test and pelvic exam
Symptoms present for more than 48 hours with concern for perforation
hard: Older adult with mild pain, little or no fever, and a near-normal white count
Pregnant patient with right flank or upper right quadrant pain and nausea attributed to pregnancy
Toddler who is irritable, vomiting, and refusing to walk, unable to describe the pain
Patient with obesity and a less impressive exam than the underlying disease
Presentation after perforation with diffuse pain and a rigid abdomen
